title: 'Gateless Barrier, Case 46: Shih-shuang: "Step from the Top of the Pole"'
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 46 of the Gateless Barrier, in which Shih-shuang asks how to take the next step from the top of a hundred-foot pole, and Changsha answers that those who sit there have entered the way but are not yet genuine. After opening with appreciation for the joint sesshin with Seattle Soto Zen and for Jeff Kelly, who proposed it, Nomon reads the pole first as a picture of rising above a messy life, then as the wobble of a mind facing a hard decision and wanting certainty. Nomon closes with Suzuki Roshi's comment from Not Always So, that the pole has no top, and the practice is to say yes and walk into the kitchen for breakfast.
topics: koan about sitting on a 100-foot pole

sentences.text: Good morning everybody.
I want to say a few words of appreciation first, and I want to say why I want to do that too.
I don't know that it's particularly important that you hear about what this particular individual is appreciating; I just seem to have the job open my mouth right now.

But I think it is the job of the speaker, whoever the speaker is in that moment, to remind us of our own bigger self, deeper self, that we help each other by bringing up good qualities like appreciation and gratitude.
We're pretty darn quick at bringing up the not-so-good qualities, so we have to be more deliberate, I think, and balance it out.
It helps to have the structure like a dharma talk, where I know I'm not supposed to complain about politics or something like that.
I know the job is to bring up appreciation, but I try to do it on all of our behalf, not because I want you to know what I care about or something like that.

One thing is I really appreciate that we have this joint sesshin with Seattle Soto Zen, and it's wonderful we have several people from that sangha here, some of whom come, dare I say, religiously every year.
It's wonderful to have Kanji and Alison here for the first time, I think.
We've got the gig helping that sangha, much to her surprise, well-deserved surprise.
This makes me want to bring up Jeff Kelly, because he was the teacher before of that sangha.
These combined sesshin were really his idea; he's such a great proponent of sesshin practice.
I think he hit town and knew that he didn't quite have the resources to do sesshin on his own, or with the group in Seattle, and that it would be great to team up.
At first, he wanted to instantly make this a seven-day sesshin, which is traditional, or even eight days.
You start on the first of December and you end on the morning of the eighth, like seven and a half, I guess.
Because the morning of the eighth is in the tradition, just like Christmas.
Just like Christmas is December twenty-fifth, December eighth is the morning the Buddha awakened, so that's when you end your Rohatsu sesshin.
That doesn't quite match our conventional reality, and we don't think we could try it.
Hopefully, some of us would come.
But this works pretty well, about half that amount of time.
Then we just got lucky this year; the morning of the eighth is the first Sunday of December, so it's kind of great.
Anyway, Jeff had to step back from active practice for his own health, which is a good reminder: practice doesn't solve everything.
All kinds of things it helps with.
I'm sure he wouldn't mind me sharing that for some reason he doesn't understand why completely.
Practicing this actively and leading a Zen sangha was not helping him, so he stepped away.
But he's here in spirit, and such appreciation, like so much appreciation, this I'm pretty confident I can say on our behalf.
Don't you appreciate everyone else here?
We could never pull this off without every single one of us.
It's not just like the job assignments and blah blah blah, although that's true.
It's just our presence and our spirit, even if it's like a seemingly semi-random mix of different particular manifestations.
You're like, wait a minute, I'm here for the first time, you're not talking about me.
No, I am, I am.
We need the dyed-in-the-wool regulars and the new people and everything in between.
We need all these positions, and we've inherited this wonderfully rich opportunity to create this society.
We create a society together with all the pieces that it needs.
And we can only do that completely with all of us, so I appreciate that so much.
It's amazing how we pull this off; we don't even know how to pull it off, and yet, we do.
I also want to appreciate the reality that's true for me and I bet for you: that we show up here a little bit messed up.
You know what I mean?
A little bit dysregulated, a little bit edgy or confused or tired or stressed or something.
There's always something going on.
I don't know about you, but I'm always surprised and new.
Like, sesshin starts, and I'm feeling whatever kind of everyday feelings I'm having, which involves a certain amount of suffering and confusion.
Sesshin starts, and I have this powerful feeling of, oh yeah, I heard someone say even before I said that, oh yeah, it's okay.
It's okay.
And somehow that feeling of oh yeah, it's okay that sesshin supports, which is in us.
Anyway, I don't know if it's magical to sesshin, but it's supported by sesshin.
Some of that feeling really requires a community.
Maybe I'd kind of chill out after a while if I went and did a four-day solo retreat, and that would probably be good to do too.
I don't think I'd have that quality of sitting down last night, the zendo full to burst in, although we found out later half the people were like, what?
Bye.
Didn't matter, didn't matter.
They were still there creating sesshin.
You know, that first minute sitting down, didn't you feel that?
And it can coexist with like, what the hell am I doing here?
Or this is going to be too hard or something else for sure.
But I think that's there, don't you think?
So I appreciate that the most of all: that we can show up all kind of dysregulated in all kinds of ways, and together, I don't know what, like we harmonize or something, we get a harmonic tune up.
Anyway, I want to bring up another old Zen story, which I think kind of relates to all this.
I've been doing this project, if you haven't been here, of giving a talk on all forty-eight stories in the most famous collection called Mumonkan, the gateless barrier collection.
I'm skipping ahead a little bit.

I'm actually supposed to do, like, I skipped twenty-four somehow, so I'm going to go back and get twenty-four, but somehow I had to jump ahead to forty-six because this particular story has been kind of resonating in my mind for a while, and I haven't done it yet, so who says it had to be in order?
So here's case forty-six from the Mumonkan.
Shershuang Chanmaster said, *When standing at the top of a hundred-foot pole, how do you take the next step?*
Another teacher of old said, *You who sit on top of a hundred-foot pole, although you have entered the way, you are not yet genuine.
Take a step from the top of the pole, and the worlds of the ten directions are your complete body.* So it's basically two quotations, connected quotations, this story.
Master Shershuang said, *When standing on the top of a hundred-foot pole, how do you take the next step?*
Another eminent teacher, turns out to be named Changsha, said, *You who sit at the top of the hundred-foot pole, although you have entered the way, you are not yet genuine.

Take a step from the top of the pole, and the worlds of the ten directions are your complete body.* The first master mentioned is from the eleventh century; these are Chinese Chanmasters, tradition we call Zen.
Shershuang was the eleventh century, and then the other teacher, Changsha, is the eighth century.
The fun thing about these stories is they let people in different centuries be in conversation, be in the same room.
It helps us with our linear idea of time, which is probably one of the big roots of our suffering anyway.
There's something great in these stories, just about the fluidity of time.

Oftentimes it'll say a whole story, and then it'll say later, so-and-so was talking to so-and-so about the first part, and our mind assumes the next day, or that afternoon, or something like that, and then you look up the references and you find out it's like four hundred years later.
You remember that time when master so-and-so was saying such-and-so?
I've been thinking about that.
Oh yeah, me too.
So here we are down, well now we're sort of different, but before we arrived here, we were down there, weren't we, in the busy ground of our life.

We so easily lose perspective sometimes, and we forget we have any other real choice than to just pretty much slog along as best we can, to react to things that we react to, to have our moments of happiness and ease here and there, but then we so easily get distracted and a little annoyed, and we also get really good at putting kind of a good face in the whole thing, right?
You know, someone asks you how you are, oh fine, fine.
We more or less accept it, but it's messy, you know, our actual life, right?
It's kind of messy.
It's okay, you know, it's workable, but it's hard, and on we go.
But isn't it interesting the way we also so desire a different perspective?
We don't always think of that when we're kind of slogging down below, but it's interesting the way in spiritual practice there are so many metaphors that are about rising above, right?
It's like so common you don't even think about it; it's like, yeah, that's how it is.
That's a metaphor, right?
That progress is rising above it all.
Progress is climbing the mountain.
Finding a lofty perspective, like a lofty perspective is definitely better than a low perspective.
We all know that.
So it's interesting that's so common.
Heaven is up above, right?
And we know what's down below.
It's also interesting that there's a theme there, especially in the Chinese tradition and the Christian tradition too, where they're more like going out into the desert.
But anyway, a theme of wildness too: that our crazy lowlands life in town with commerce and busyness and intense relationships everywhere is different from the wildness of the mountains.
When we're walking along a path on a rocky mountain with the company of alpine plants and the winds and the clouds and the endless views, there's nothing there but perspective.
Our problems fade away.
So it's interesting; we seem to have this innate desire for being above our own life, for perspective.
And yet we can't seem to live there.
We can't live on top of the mountain.
Maybe a few people can, but not most of us.
We also need each other.
We need the lowlands.
We need the hustle and bustle.
We need relationships, and that's where the jobs are anyway; we need that.
So this koan talking about a one-hundred-foot pole is kind of interesting because here perspective seems to be symbolized not by a mountain or a monastery.
So many of these stories are about a monk arriving at a monastery, which is also arriving at perspective, or the possibility of a new perspective.
The conversation with the teacher is a conversation on perspective; it's a rising above.
And that's also why all Zen and Chan monasteries always have a mountain name, even if the mountain is like a low hill kind of thing, they have a lofty mountain name because it's about perspective.
So here the perspective is not gained by climbing a mountain, but by somehow shimming up a one-hundred-foot pole.
And somehow this pole is just balanced on the ground; it doesn't fall over.
You climb up really carefully.
It's not the same as summiting Baker, but being one-hundred feet above everything is pretty lofty.
Everything looks different.
Your usual world scurries along below you, and you're definitely a new person on top of the one-hundred-foot pole.
And this idea of being a new person is also interesting because it helps to daylight our assumptions about being a person too.
That when we're scurrying around in a busy life, I'm using this metaphor, the lowlands, but you know what I mean, nothing wrong with the lowlands either.
But anyway, in our day-to-day life, we think our personhood is kind of fixed, maybe it's just being continually reconditioned.
Seems similar to the last person here: I am again.
But then when we change conditions by being on top of our pole having perspective, it seems like a whole new person.
But maybe it just points out that it's always a new person.
In any case, whatever it is we are, that person, somehow we manage to get some perspective.
We've climbed the one-hundred-foot pole, and there's this new sense of things.
Why was I worried about all that stuff down there?
What was my problem?
But the moment after you realize that, you notice that you're balanced on this skinny little pole, and you get tense, right?
You start teetering.
They may be our really big important problems: what was I talking about?
Life is hard.
I'm going to fall any moment now.
I think that's the other challenge for us: we would like a new perspective that's also stable and fixed.
It turns out it's also radically fluid and changing and won't stay stable, so we have a problem.
We want the perspective that when we get there, it freaks us out because we're also teetering on this pole.
And it's hard for us to taste freedom and then lose it again.
So hard.
But the interesting thing about this koan is it's suggesting that we can have some stability on top of the one-hundred-foot pole.
The first master says, you who sit on top of the one-hundred-foot pole.
I'm sorry, it's the second master, the earlier master, excuse me, the second one in the story, Changsha.
He says, *You who sit on top of the one-hundred-foot pole.* So this word sit matters, of course.
Sit, not stand, not balance, not teeter, not figure it out.
But sit.
This is a deep thread in our practice.
Sitting means that there is somehow a stability and instability, an allowing of fluidity.
We don't know who we are when we sit, but we can sit, and we can sit through anything, really.
That's the amazing thing.
I'm sure everybody here has sat through.
Some very difficult things.
Which doesn't always mean physically sitting on a cushion; it's a way of being, right?
It's a spirit.
We can even sit through our own death.
Maybe you or I don't have a conscious memory of sitting through our own death, but I'm quite confident that we will and we can.
Many of us have had the opportunity to sit with others in their last moments.
It's hard, but it's so beautiful.
So that's true sitting.
It's okay that the pole is the way it is.
It's okay that we are the way we are.
Every moment just as it needs to be.
There's a vast perspective, and we don't need any perspective or all perspectives.
And then we can do that on top of a one-hundred-foot pole.
So that's awesome.
The earlier Master praises those who sit on top of the one-hundred-foot pole.
Maybe we all have heard that this is our practice in some way here: sitting with uncertainty, sitting with instability.
But he goes on to say that's not quite enough.
He said, "You who sit on the one-hundred-foot pole, although you have entered the way, you are not yet genuine."
Entered the way.
That sounds good, but not yet genuine.
So in our tradition, there's always this urging to go beyond.
What's the deal with that anyway?
We're just getting set up here for perfectionism, being like Zen overachievers: go beyond!
Dogen's constantly saying this, right?
You think your understanding is complete, but no, here's what that means: you've barely glimpsed the outer edges of the whole territory.
Study deeper.
Keep going.
So it seems like this Master Changsha is saying the same thing, but he has an instruction, though, thankfully.
Dogen is just like, "Study deeper."
Like, okay, I'll try.
Thanks, boss.
I'll tell you how to do it.
So here the instruction is: step off.
"You who sit on the top of the one-hundred-foot pole, although you've entered the way, you're not yet genuine.
Take a step from the top of the pole.
Take a step.
And the worlds of the ten directions are completely your body."
So let it all go is a useful, simple reading, I think.
That's okay.
Think hard.
Practice hard.
Think we're attaining something: stability or something.
And realize that was only provisional.
You know, that was only to encourage us.
That was like a phantom city on the horizon.
Then we really have to trust and step off the pole.
Let go of having a lofty perspective.
Let go of perspective altogether.
Some reason made me think of that line in the ordination ceremony where it encourages us that we are going beyond the karma of body, speech, and mind.
Going beyond the karma of body, speech, and mind.
Going beyond understanding.
Going beyond action.
Going on beyond inaction.
Stepping off the pole.

So I think that's the more or less usual way of talking about this case: that on the one hand we really can and probably should learn how to climb this pole, how to climb the shaky, shaky pole of our life.
Have a broader perspective.
Stop getting so stuck in this little stuff, you know, and be stable even as the pole wavers in the wind.
At least for a time because everything's fluid and everything's impermanent.
And that being stable and elevated even in the midst of the chaos of this world is so helpful, right?
So important.
Good for you and good for everybody that you're in contact with, which is also to say the whole world.
A gift, you know, a gift to do this at work, inner work, if you will.
And learn how to climb on top of the pole and sit.
But that's only in the beginning.
That's like the prequel.
And the main event is stepping off.
Letting go.
Trusting with your whole body and mind that wherever you land is just where you need to land.
And as you plunge back to the lowlands and you might land hard, you know, one hundred feet is pretty high.
But after you land you can dust yourself off and continue your work in the world.
And really see that the lowlands and the mountains aren't that different after all.
And there's stuff that needs attending to: there are trains to load and fields to plow and children to feed and children to try to get through high school.
But this case also came up in my mind in a different way, so I want to mention that too with a different slant.
And I especially want to mention that too because I think it would be a mistake to limit ourselves too much with all these wonderful teachings that we are so lucky.
How lucky can we be to have access to these quirky, weird, hard stories, you know?
And it's good that they're kind of hard too, I think.
How's it going for us to just seek out easy?
You know, like we've created the culture of easy.
But anyway, when they occur to us in one way or the other way to just be curious, even if later we figure out, "Wait a minute, that's not what it means.
That's wrong."
Doesn't matter.
Koans don't have a right or wrong.
So it's great, I think, when this stuff pops into your mind and you can turn it over no matter which way you turn it over and not worry too much about whether it's the so-called usual understanding.
So I was thinking about this story of the one-hundred-foot pole in terms of making difficult life decisions.
Let's see if you can relate to this or not.
One of the things I've noticed is that when my mind is faced with any kind of a difficult decision, it really hates the uncertainty of it.

If I have to choose, and I think oftentimes the urgency that I feel around the choice is probably a little bit off, but I feel some urgency, and I have to choose between this way or that way, I notice that my mind really doesn't like the wobbling on top of the pole part.
Do you have this?
Because I want to know what's the right choice.
I want to get off of here as soon as possible, but only if I jump in the right direction.
And then the pole goes this way and that way, and I'm like, "Whoa, whoa, whoa, is it this direction?"
"Whoa, no, it's this direction."
It's really difficult.
It's really disorienting.
And I think the difficulty is not so much the pole or the life choice because we will all be faced with so many life choices and away.
What a blessing that we have choices.
What I'm noticing for myself is the difficulty is the mind that's not willing to hang out on the pole.
It doesn't want that.
The mind that's churning, trying to imagine future outcomes from decision A or decision B.
Because the minute the mind starts trying to visualize exactly what will happen if I make this choice instead of that choice, it kind of locks down in some way and gets heavier.
And it's like the pole bends more, and then it's scary, "I'm going to fall off before I really decide to get," and then it bends back the other way.

So I'm really getting interested in being on the pole and also trying not to get too involved with being embarrassed by this crazy tendency of mind that even after however many years of training in this ability of Zen and all these darn stories about not knowing is most intimate rest in uncertainty.
Bodhidharma said, "Don't know!"
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
I want to know.
You know what I mean?
So I'm starting to learn, I think, that it's not so much which choice to make or that I can even figure out which choice to take, although our choices really matter, karma is real.

But that the practice, this way of looking at the practice on top of the one-hundred-foot pole is more like, "Can I be kinder, more patient, more compassionate with that part of me that wants certainty and is afraid of uncertainty?"

And when I can lighten that up, not so heavy, and I can just flow with the vagaries of the mind, with the vagaries of circumstance, with the vagaries of the pole, with the way that everything is changing.
So maybe in the end these two ways of looking at the koan are not really all that different, just different ways of looking at it.
Here's a third and final way to look at it.
This is from Suzuki Roshi.
This is one of those stories that every Zen teacher has commented on sooner or later.

If he stays on the top, he's not the enlightened one.
When he jumps off the top of the pole, he may be the enlightened one.
How we understand this koan is how we understand our practice.
The reason we believe that evil desires should be thrown out is because we stay at the top of the pole."
Then we have a problem.
The reason we believe that evil desires should be thrown out because we stay at the top of the pole.
Then we have a problem.
Actually, there is no top of the pole.
The pole continues forever.
So you cannot stop there.
But when you have some experience of enlightenment, you may think that you can rest there, observing various sights from the top of the pole.
But things are continuously growing or changing into something else.
Nothing exists in its own form or color.
When you think, "Here is the top," then you will have a problem: the problem of whether or not to jump off.
But you cannot jump off from here.
That is already a misunderstanding.
It is not possible.
And even though you try to stop at the top of the pole, you cannot stay there because it is growing continuously.
That is the problem.
So, forget about stepping off the top of the pole.
To forget about the top of the pole is to be right where you are now.
To be this way or that way, not to be in the past or the future, not to have this outcome or that outcome, but to be right here.

This is Zazen.

There is no problem.

You forget all about yourself and are refreshed.
You are a new self, and before that self becomes the old self, you say yes, and you walk into the kitchen for breakfast.
We better hear that again.
Isn't it wonderful?
Sometimes what you really needed turned out to be some odd, confusing teaching from a great teacher.
It didn't make sense in that usual way.
There is a feeling to it.
Let's hear that again and then we'll close.
Suzuki Roshi on evil desires.

When he jumps off, he may be the enlightened one.

That is the problem.
So, here is the practice instruction from Suzuki Roshi.
See if we can practice that, the sesshin.
Here it is: forget about stopping at the top of the pole.
Forget about the top of the pole is to be right where you are now.
Not to be this way or that way.
Not to be in the past or the future.
Not to take this choice or that choice.
Not to take that choice, but to be right here.
Do you understand?

Forget this moment and grow into the next.
The secret is just to say yes and jump off from here.
Then there is no problem.
It means to be yourself in the present moment, always yourself without sticking to an old self.
You forget about yourself and you are refreshed.
Forget about yourself.

Before that self becomes an old self, you say yes, and you walk to the kitchen for breakfast.
So, we have just gotten started in a way.
In a way we have always been here.
Let's see if we can follow this great teaching from Suzuki Roshi.
We are on the pole and yet the pole is endless.
